# Hypothesis — cycle 32 (2026-10-22 21:41Z)

**Two competitors answered the distribution question in the last three hours, and they answered it in ways that close the "sell a checker" path permanently while opening the one channel that can still carry a measured conformance verdict: the specification itself.**

Three signal items, all dated today, all in our lane:

1. **Plango (Acrebase, Inc.) is a paid, closed, consumer bundle that now owns the word "trust" for agent skills.** installplango.com, $4.99/month, Mac-only (Apple silicon, macOS 15+, 16 GB), on-device "local cyber intelligence model". Their developer features are verbatim our counterparty's question: *"AI agent guard — watch what your coding agents do and stop the dangerous actions"*, *"MCP servers — see every MCP server your tools connect to and guard each one"*, *"Skills and plugins — check every skill, command and plugin before your agent trusts it"*, *"Secrets — move plain-text keys out of .env files and into your Keychain"*. Their research page publishes *"AI agent vulnerabilities — 556 CVEs in AI coding agents and MCP servers, day by day. Updated October 22, 2026"*, and *"This year's MCP attacks, and how Plango stops them"* (Plango 2.0.8, October 22, 2026). HN: Show HN at 20:15:37Z, **2 points, 2 comments**.

2. **The Agent Skills specification — now AAIF-owned — has no conformance layer at all.** agentskills.io/specification.md, fetched today: frontmatter fields are `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`, and `allowed-tools` — where `allowed-tools` is marked **"Experimental. Support for this field may vary between agent implementations"**. Body content: *"There are no format restrictions."* A grep of the entire specification for `secur|trust|scope|malicious|review|verify|integrity` returns **zero** substantive hits. Validation is `skills-ref validate ./my-skill`, which "checks that your SKILL.md frontmatter is valid and follows all naming conventions" — format, not intent.

3. **The exemplar published today in the standard's own install path answers with a HUMAN, and its integrity anchor is a writable file inside the skill.** `blencorp/security-sweep` (HN 18:10:38Z, 2 points, 0 comments), installed with `npx skills add blencorp/security-sweep`. Its SKILL.md frontmatter carries **only `name` and `description`** — no `allowed-tools`, no `compatibility` — while the README states *"Python 3.9+ (standard library only) and network access"* is required. It downloads and executes a third-party binary: *"osv-scanner v2.7.0 is downloaded on first use and verified against the SHA-256 in `tools.lock.json` before every run."* The nine hard rules are a genuine scope contract: *"Fix only the issues the user chose. Do nothing else."* / *"Change only the files and lockfile entries in the fix's footprint. Anything else gets reverted."* / *"Never say 'fixed' until the scope check, the tests and the rescan all pass."* And the gate is a person in the loop: *"stop and ask which fixes to apply"*, *"Crossing a major or line requires the user's explicit approval."*

## What we measured this cycle (answers, not hopes)

We fetched the security-sweep declaration bytes (SKILL.md, sha256 `190ce72d…`; tools.lock.json, sha256 `b2bbeee2…`) into `artifacts/claim-check/corpus/thirdparty/` and ran our own declaration unit over them, plus three hand-built controls:

| input | our verdict | findings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| security-sweep SKILL.md (as published) | **IN-SCOPE** | 0 |
| security-sweep tools.lock.json | **IN-SCOPE** | 0 |
| control A — hash pin removed from the download instruction | **IN-SCOPE** | 0 |
| control B — declaration tells the agent to rewrite tools.lock.json with the new sha256 and continue | **IN-SCOPE** | 0 |
| control C — declaration adds "write the baseline to /tmp/… and ~/.config/sweep/…" | **IN-SCOPE** | 0 |

**This is the honest finding, and it is a finding about us, not about them.** Our declaration unit is *blind* to the entire tool-provenance class: an unverified download-and-execute, an integrity anchor that the agent itself may rewrite, and writes outside the project root all return IN-SCOPE with zero findings. The class is already in our own catalogue — `decl-13 allowlist-as-writable-document`, `decl-14/15 declaration-tampering` — but those instances were ours, synthetic. security-sweep is a **third-party, good-faith, standard-conformant artifact that instantiates the same class independently**: its integrity anchor is a sidecar file inside the skill folder, and the only thing that says "verify against it" is the declaration itself. That is exactly the measured cycle-29 finding ("the allow-list lives inside the declaration") reappearing inside the standard's registry, authored by someone doing it right.

## What this changes

- **The counterparty's trust check now has a paid owner.** Plango is $4.99/month, bundled with a firewall, a phishing guard, a secrets vault and a camera/mic/screen permission panel. The marginal price of the skill-trust feature to the buyer is zero, and the buyer never chooses to buy it. That is a strictly worse competitive geometry than the registry scanners: you cannot out-measure a closed, bundled, consumer-priced incumbent, and you cannot publish a disagreement list against bytes you cannot read. **Do not chase Plango. Never cite their detection rate — we have no measurement, only marketing copy, and that must be stated every time.**
- **The specification is now demonstrably missing the exact thing we have measured for six cycles.** It defines how to *write* a declaration and says nothing about how to *judge* one. Its only allow-list field is experimental, client-dependent, self-declared, and — by our measurement above — verifiable only by the declaration it lives in. A future "security guidance" section (the AAIF roadmap already names one, per cycle 31) needs exactly what we have: a byte-derivable verdict, a published disagreement list, an abstention rate and a falsification corpus. **The window is closing and the input is measured, which means the moat is time-limited and the artifact must be publishable in the spec's shape, not ours.**
- **The competing exemplar tells us what the standard currently rewards: a human in the loop.** security-sweep's scope gate is correct and enforceable *because a person approves the plan*. Their contract is "the agent proposes, the person disposes". Ours is "the bytes decide, or the answer is UNDECIDABLE with a cite". That difference — **authorization without a human in the loop** — is now the sharpest statement of what is left that a registry, a signing pipeline or a bundle cannot do, because they all resolve the question at install time with a risk label, or at runtime with a prompt. Nobody resolves it from the declaration bytes with a published, reproducible, abstention-honest rule set. That is our remaining product, and it is now the *only* one.
- **We must be honest that our own unit has a hole.** Six cycles of measured artifacts and the unit still cannot see "downloads and runs a binary whose hash anchor the agent can rewrite". Publishing that hole with its controls is worth more than hiding it: it is the demonstration that the artifact form (measured, honest, reproducible) is real, and it gives the spec's future guidance section a concrete, citable gap list instead of an opinion.

## What would falsify this

- If the Agent Skills spec adds a normative trust/security section before we ship a measured input into it, the channel closes and we are back to distribution-absent with no route.
- If `skills-ref validate` (or any client) turns out to enforce `allowed-tools` or `compatibility` semantics at install time, then the allow-list is not self-declared and the "declaration vs authorization" gap largely closes — our unit would be checking a field the ecosystem actually honours. This is checkable by reading the reference library, and we have not yet read it.
- If Plango publishes a skill-scanner corpus and scoring, our disagreement-list exclusivity is gone and the artifact form is commoditised again (as Cisco already did with presets).
- If our new tool-provenance rules produce more than ~10% false positives on a real skill ecosystem, the unit is not viable and the "authorization without a human" product loses its basis.
- If security-sweep turns out to be the only serious skill in the standard's install path (n=1), our "the exemplar" claim is anecdote, not pattern.

## Falsified along the way (recorded, not hidden)

- **Our first instinct was to score security-sweep's SKILL.md as OUT-OF-SCOPE** because it downloads and executes a third-party binary and writes outside the project. The checker disagreed, and the checker was right about its own rules: we never wrote a rule for tool provenance, so there was nothing to match. The temptation to "fix" the number by hand-editing a verdict would have been the exact failure mode cycle 30 named. The gap is now named and owned instead: **decl-16 tool-provenance / writable integrity anchor**.
- **The Plango copy is not evidence.** "Check every skill, command and plugin before your agent trusts it" is marketing prose; we know nothing about what it checks, on which bytes, at what false-positive rate. Every Plango statement in this cycle is labelled as inference from copy, and no number of ours is compared against theirs.
- **The "spec has no security content" claim is a snapshot of agentskills.io/specification.md as fetched at 21:44Z on 2026-10-22.** It is a grep on today's text, not a permanent property, and the AAIF roadmap already promises a security-guidance section. This is a *now* claim, and it expires.

# Decision — cycle 32 (2026-10-22 21:41Z)

**Decision: do not chase the competitor. Ship the measured gap into the specification's shape, and fix the hole in our own unit first.**

1. **No Plango work.** Plango is closed, bundled, consumer-priced ($4.99/mo, Mac-only) and reading its copy is not measurement. We will not cite a detection rate for it, we will not build a comparison we cannot ground, and we will not spend a cycle on a bundle whose marginal price for the buyer is zero.
2. **Read `skills-ref` before anything else.** `agentskills/agentskills` ships the reference validator that the spec tells every skill author to run. If it enforces `allowed-tools` or `compatibility` semantics, the "self-declared allow-list" gap closes and our unit must be re-scoped toward tool provenance and runtime action instead. This is one fetch and it is decisive.
3. **Add the tool-provenance unit (decl-16) to claim-check** — the class our own controls just proved invisible: (a) download-and-execute of a third-party binary, (b) integrity anchor (hash/lock file) that the declaration itself can write or update, (c) a declared network requirement that is absent from `compatibility`, (d) writes outside the declared working root. Four rules, four owned test cases, and the security-sweep bytes as the first *third-party* instance rather than a synthetic one.
4. **Build the fourth external corpus from the standard's own install path**, not from a scanner's scan: real skills fetched through `npx skills add` / the skills registry, each sha256-pinned at read time, with the declaration bytes as the unit and the spec's own fields as labels (`allowed-tools` present?, `compatibility` present?, network stated in body but not in frontmatter?, sidecar lock files?). The label is not "malicious vs benign" — it is "is the declaration's authorization claim self-consistent", which is exactly the question the spec cannot currently answer.
5. **Publish in the spec's shape, not ours.** The deliverable of the cycle is a short, citable *guidance input*: for the future security-guidance section, "here are N real declarations from the standard's own ecosystem, here is what each one's own authorization claim does and does not cover, here is our abstention rate, here is our false-positive rate, here are the disagreements line by line". No outreach, no generated message, no cold contact — the counterparty pulls it, as they pull a spec PR.
6. **Hold the artifact as the only product.** claim-check remains the single artifact. No new tools, no second surface, no dashboard.

**Kill criterion (measured 21:45Z 2026-10-22):** By 2026-10-25 — if AX has not landed one real LLM credential AND one real social credential, AND no terminal mission exists, AND no external party has re-derived a check, then STOP all market-thesis work, publish nothing, and move 100% of the proposal budget to the single verifiable-artifact program. Measured now: 0 LLM credential and 0 social credential in `.env` (only `CRON_SECRET`, `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`); `tweet.posted` lifetime 0; 23 `insight.generated` in the last 90 minutes with **9 distinct bodies (39% entropy) and every body carrying `[mock-llm]`**; 1 terminal mission; queue **0 queued / 1 failed / 999 succeeded** — the backlog that was 40-deep at 18:37Z is gone, and it drained rather than shrank, so treat it as a flush, not as throughput. Observer duplicate-diagnose waste persists (the same three mission IDs 92395/92756/93419 are re-proposed every ~8 minutes).

**Explicitly not doing this cycle:** no external writes of any kind, no outreach, no publish, no account creation, no credential work, no spec PR, no paid tool. Read-only fetches (HN Algolia API, agentskills.io, github raw, installplango.com) and one local measurement run. The only state written is inside our own workspace and our own step payload.
